# Reporting & the Shared Render Engine {#sec-reporting}

A recurring need in surveillance work is to turn an investigation into a
document: the plots, the isolate tables, the AMR findings and the provenance,
collected into a single PDF or HTML report to circulate or archive. This chapter
describes the **design** for that report function and the engine it is built on —
the same Quarto toolchain that renders the PhyloTrace manuals.

::: {.callout-note title="Status — a planned feature on existing foundations"}
At the time of writing, the in-app report generator is a design, not a shipped
panel. This chapter documents the intended shape and the building blocks already
in the codebase that it composes. It is placed here so the manuals and the report
function share one engine and one set of conventions from the start.
:::

## One engine for two jobs {#sec-report-engine}

The deliberate decision is to render the report with the **same engine that
renders these manuals**: Quarto. This avoids adding a parallel toolchain, and it
means everything true of the books — clickable
tables of contents, cross-references, HTML *and* PDF from one source, syntax and
figure handling — is available to reports at no additional engineering cost.
HTML output is self-contained; PDF output uses the `tinytex`/LaTeX toolchain
the app already depends on (@sec-install).

## The building blocks already in place {#sec-report-blocks}

A report assembles outputs PhyloTrace already produces, so most of the
implementation already exists:

- **Publication-quality plots** — `app/logic/viz_export.R` (@sec-tech-viz-export)
  already renders any engine's plot to PDF/SVG/PNG at a requested physical size
  and DPI (ggplot engines by server re-render; MST/Map by genuine
  high-resolution client capture). A report embeds these directly.
- **A saved investigation** — an Analysis (@sec-tech-dashboard) is already a named set
  of plots, each with its full `inputs_json` snapshot and a thumbnail, persisted
  in the database. An Analysis is, in effect, the *contents list* of a report.
- **Tabular results** — the metadata table, the classical-MLST and AMR wide views
  (@sec-db-companions), and the `typing_provenance` rows (@sec-tech-typing-provenance)
  are all already queryable as data frames ready to print.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-report
%%| fig-cap: "The report function composes existing outputs through the Quarto engine — the same one that builds these manuals."
flowchart LR
  AN["Analysis<br/>(saved plots + selection)"] --> RPT["parameterised<br/>Quarto/rmarkdown doc"]
  VE["viz_export.R<br/>plot images"] --> RPT
  TB["metadata · MLST · AMR ·<br/>provenance tables"] --> RPT
  RPT --> H["report.html<br/>(self-contained)"]
  RPT --> P["report.pdf<br/>(tinytex)"]
```

## The intended flow {#sec-report-flow}

The natural implementation is a **parameterised** render, the canonical Shiny
"download report" pattern: a template document takes an Analysis id (or an
explicit isolate selection) as a parameter, queries the plots and tables for it,
and renders to the chosen format inside a `downloadHandler`. Because the template
is plain Quarto/rmarkdown, adding a section is editing a document, not the app.

::: {.callout-important title="A report is a reproducible artifact"}
Because an Analysis stores the exact inputs behind every plot, a report generated
from it is *reproducible*: regenerating it later against the same database
yields the same figures. Because provenance also travels in the database
(@sec-tech-typing-provenance), a report can state, per isolate, the scheme and tool
versions that produced its calls — the kind of methods detail a publication or an
accreditation audit needs.
:::

## Chapter summary

- The report function is planned to reuse the manuals' Quarto engine, giving
  self-contained HTML and `tinytex` PDF from one template.
- Its ingredients already exist: `viz_export.R` for publication-quality figures,
  `analysis_store.R` for the saved plot set, and the existing table readers for
  metadata/MLST/AMR/provenance.
- The intended mechanism is a parameterised render over an Analysis, driven from a
  `downloadHandler`.

The remaining operations chapters cover installing and running the app
(@sec-install), testing it (@sec-testing), and extending it (@sec-extending).
